summary: Specifies how Ethernet frames are wrapped and carried across an MPLS network inside a pseudowire. This lets providers offer an emulated point-to-point Ethernet service over networks they already run. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Putting an Ethernet message in an envelope so it can ride a different delivery network and come out the other end unchanged, as if on one long cable.

questions: raw mode vs tagged mode pseudowire
what is the pseudowire control word
subtitle: How Ethernet frames are wrapped, tagged or untagged, and carried over an MPLS network as if across one long cable.

tldr.problem: Service providers want to offer Ethernet connectivity between two customer sites over an MPLS network they already run.
tldr.mechanism: An Ethernet pseudowire carries each frame, minus preamble and FCS, with an optional control word, a pseudowire label and the tunnel encapsulation. It runs in raw mode or tagged mode, and emulates a single link between exactly two endpoints.
tldr.outcome: The result is an emulated point-to-point Ethernet service. This RFC is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 5462 and RFC 8469.

facts.label: Control word size
facts.value: 32 bits (4-bit zero field, reserved bits, 16-bit sequence number)

facts.label: PSN MTU headroom
facts.value: Likely 8 or more bytes greater than the largest frame

today: RFC 4448 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 5462 and RFC 8469, so read it together with those documents. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Ethernet Over MPLS
sections.content:
An Ethernet pseudowire (PW) carries Ethernet/802.3 protocol data units over an MPLS network. It assumes the PW has already been set up by a control protocol and conforms to the architecture in RFC 3985. The unit carried is the destination address, source address, length/type, MAC client data and padding of a MAC frame, in their original order.

The RFC covers the frame format used in the PW, the procedures that give a pair of customer edge (CE) routers an emulated point-to-point Ethernet service, Ethernet-specific QoS and security considerations, and inter-domain transport. Strictly the emulated service is a bridged LAN, but the procedures only support two CEs, so it is called emulated point-to-point Ethernet. Emulating LANs with more than two CEs is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Two offices want to feel like they share one cable even though a big delivery network sits between them. This memo explains how to make that trick work.

sections.title: The Reference Model
sections.content:
Customer equipment (CE1 and CE2) connects to provider edge routers (PE1 and PE2) over attachment circuits that offer a native Ethernet service. Between the PEs, a PSN tunnel carries the pseudowire. PE1 is called the ingress router and PE2 the egress router: a layer 2 PDU is received at PE1, encapsulated, transported, decapsulated at PE2 and sent out on PE2's attachment circuit.

Inside a PE, frames pass through Native Service Processing (NSP), then PW termination, then the PSN tunnel. The NSP does frame processing that may include stripping, overwriting or adding VLAN tags, port multiplexing, policing and shaping. The PW terminates at a logical port that delivers each frame unaltered to the matching point at the other end. The mechanisms are agnostic to what lies beneath the pseudowire.
sections.plainLanguage: Each office has a mail room at the edge of the delivery network. The mail room puts letters in the special envelopes and takes them out again.

sections.title: Raw Mode and Tagged Mode
sections.content:
An Ethernet PW works in one of two modes. In tagged mode (PW type 0x0004) every frame MUST carry a service-delimiting 802.1Q VLAN tag that the NSPs at both ends understand. In raw mode (PW type 0x0005) all frames from the attachment circuit go over a single PW, and service-delimiting tags are never sent over it.

A tag is service-delimiting when provider equipment added it to tell customers apart; local configuration decides this. In raw mode, such a tag MUST be stripped before the frame enters the PW. In tagged mode, if the frame has no such tag the PE prepends a dummy VLAN tag. Tagged mode is the default and the only REQUIRED mode. In both modes other tags pass through as payload, and the NSP may inspect only the outermost tag.

The 0x06 Requested VLAN ID sub-TLV is an optional 16-bit value in the LDP interface parameters. A PE that cannot rewrite the VLAN tag on output MUST use it, and it applies only to PW type 0x0004. If the ingress PE cannot comply, the PW MUST not be enabled.
sections.plainLanguage: Raw mode sends the letter exactly as it is. Tagged mode makes sure every letter wears a sticker saying which customer it belongs to.

sections.title: Encapsulation Procedures
sections.content:
When the NSP hands a frame to the PW, the preamble and FCS are stripped, a control word is prepended if needed, the PW label (the demultiplexer) is prepended, then the tunnel encapsulation, and the packet is sent. On arrival the reverse happens, and regenerating the FCS is an NSP job. Because the FCS is not carried, payload integrity transparency may be lost, though an optional method can restore it.

Several rules follow. The PW MUST NOT be enabled unless the CE-PE MTUs are known to be the same at both ends, and a payload exceeding the destination MTU MUST be dropped. Frames with hardware-level CRC errors, framing errors or runts MUST be discarded on input. IEEE 802.3x PAUSE frames MUST NOT be carried across the PW. If the PE detects a failure on the Ethernet port, or the port is disabled, it MUST send a PW status notification.

The PSN may reorder, duplicate or drop packets. Strict frame ordering needs the control word's sequencing, and if a PW requires strict ordering that option MUST be enabled. Appendix A adds that a PE should terminate PAUSE frames locally, buffering or discarding frames while paused.
sections.plainLanguage: The mail room removes the old stamp, puts the letter in the envelope with a route label, and sends it. It does not pass along 'please slow down' notes from one office to the other.

sections.title: The Control Word
sections.content:
The control word is a 32-bit header based on the generic PW MPLS control word. It provides frame sequencing, avoids equal-cost multipath (ECMP) load balancing mistakes, and supports OAM mechanisms such as VCCV. The ECMP issue arises because routers may look at the first nibble after the label stack to guess IP: a source MAC starting with 0x4 or 0x6 could be mistaken for an IPv4 or IPv6 packet, sending a PW's packets down different paths.

The first 4 bits MUST be 0 to mark PW data. The rest of the first 16 bits are reserved, MUST be sent as 0 and MUST be ignored on receipt. The next 16 bits are a sequence number in a 16-bit unsigned circular space, where 0 means no sequence check. Processing the sequence number is OPTIONAL.

The control word is optional, because early implementations were deployed without it. Future implementations MUST be able to send and receive without it, and the egress PE MUST know, by configuration or signaling, whether the ingress PE will send one.
sections.plainLanguage: The control word is a tiny numbered tag stuck on each envelope. The numbers let the receiver notice if envelopes arrive out of order.

sections.title: QoS Considerations
sections.content:
The ingress PE MAY use the 802.1Q user priority (PRI) field to choose the QoS value of the encapsulating protocol, such as the MPLS EXP bits, and the egress PE MAY use that field when queuing frames toward the CE. A PE MUST be able to carry the PW as best-effort, and PRI bits stay transparent between PEs. If a VLAN tag is added at the PE, a default PRI of zero MUST be supported.

Beyond best effort, a PE may map one class of service per PW end service to a single-class PW, several classes to one PW with several classes, or several classes to multiple PWs. The mapping from 802.1Q classes to PSN classes depends on the customer-provider agreement, and the specific PSN values are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Some letters are marked urgent. The mail room may use those marks to decide which letters go first, but it can also treat all letters the same.

sections.title: Security and MTU Limits
sections.content:
An Ethernet PW is subject to the general security considerations of RFC 3985 and the PW control protocol. It rides on an MPLS PSN, so its security is only as good as the security of that PSN. MAC address access control and security in virtual bridging setups are out of scope.

The PSN MUST be configured with an MTU large enough for a maximum-sized Ethernet frame plus the control word, PW demultiplexer and tunnel encapsulation. With MPLS this is likely to be 8 or more bytes greater than the largest frame. Fragmentation as specified elsewhere MAY be used. Without it, an encapsulated PDU that exceeds the tunnel's MTU MUST be dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: The envelope is only as safe as the delivery trucks. And the trucks must be big enough to carry the biggest letter plus its envelope.
